summary: Defines a 16-bit encoding for identifying differentiated services Per Hop Behaviors in protocol messages. It replaces RFC 2836.

plainLanguage.summary: Differentiated Services marks packets with a small number of codepoints, but the number of distinct forwarding behaviours is not limited. This RFC defines a 16-bit code that a protocol message can use to name one behaviour, or a group of them, so that a request can travel between networks and still mean the same thing.

subtitle: A 16-bit code that names a Differentiated Services Per Hop Behavior, or a set of them, inside protocol messages.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services names forwarding behaviours with only 64 DSCP values, so a protocol message needs its own way to name a behaviour, or a set of behaviours, especially when the message crosses a management domain.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a 16-bit field with two cases: a standards-defined behaviour is encoded as its recommended DSCP value, and an experimental or local behaviour uses a 12-bit code assigned by IANA. Bit 14 marks a set rather than a single behaviour.
tldr.outcome: Any protocol that has to name a behaviour MUST use this encoding. The document replaces RFC 2836 and adds the Class Selector codepoints that the earlier version left out.

today: RFC 3140 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2001. It replaced RFC 2836 and has not been obsoleted since. The encoding it defines is the way a protocol message names a Differentiated Services behaviour, or a group of them.

sections.title: Why PHBs Need Identification Codes
sections.content:
Differentiated Services, as described in RFC 2474 and RFC 2475, introduces the notion of Per Hop Behaviors (PHBs), which define how traffic belonging to a particular behavior aggregate is treated at an individual network node. In IP packet headers, PHBs are not indicated as such; instead, Differentiated Services Codepoint (DSCP) values are used. There are only 64 possible DSCP values, but there is no such limit on the number of PHBs. In a given network domain there is a locally defined mapping between DSCP values and PHBs. Standardized PHBs recommend a DSCP mapping, but network operators may choose alternative mappings.

In some cases it is necessary or desirable to identify a particular PHB in a protocol message, such as a message negotiating bandwidth management or path selection, especially when such messages pass between management domains. Work in progress includes communication between bandwidth brokers and MPLS support of Diff-Serv.

In certain cases what needs to be identified is not an individual PHB but a set of PHBs. One example is a set of PHBs that must follow the same physical path to prevent re-ordering: the three PHBs belonging to a single Assured Forwarding class, AF11, AF12 and AF13, from RFC 2597.

This document defines a binary encoding to uniquely identify PHBs, or sets of PHBs, in protocol messages, and that encoding MUST be used when such identification is required. It replaces RFC 2836, which omitted the considerations for the Class Selector codepoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Packet headers can only carry 64 codepoints, but there are more forwarding behaviours than that, and each network can map codepoints to behaviours its own way. This document gives protocol messages a code of their own, so a request can say exactly which behaviour it wants.

sections.title: Where the Codes Are Used
sections.content:
Differentiated Services is expected to be supported over various underlying technologies, which the RFC broadly refers to as link layers. For the transport of IP packets, some of these link layers make use of connections or logical connections where the forwarding behaviour supported by each link layer device is a property of the connection. Within the link layer domain, each link layer node schedules traffic depending on which connection the traffic is transported in. Examples of such link layers include ATM and MPLS.

For efficient support of Diff-Serv over these link layers, one model is for different Behavior Aggregates (BAs), or sets of Behavior Aggregates, to be transported over different connections, so that they are granted different and appropriate forwarding behaviours inside the link layer cloud. When those connections are dynamically established for the transport of Diff-Serv traffic, it is very useful to communicate at connection establishment time what forwarding behaviour or behaviours are to be granted to each connection by the link layer device, so that the BAs transported experience consistent forwarding behaviour inside the link layer cloud. This can be achieved by including the encoding of the corresponding PHB, or set of PHBs, in the connection establishment signalling messages. Proposed use of these encodings by the RSVP and LDP label distribution protocols for Diff-Serv over MPLS is described in a work in progress.

The RFC also describes another approach: the ATM Forum has a requirement to indicate desired IP quality of service treatments in ATM signalling, so that ATM switches can be just as supportive of the desired service as IP forwarders are. To do so, a new VC call setup information element is being defined that will carry PHB identification codes.
sections.plainLanguage: The code is meant for signalling, not for packet headers. When a link layer such as ATM or MPLS sets up a connection to carry traffic, the signalling message can carry this code so the switch at the far end knows what treatment to apply.

sections.title: The 16-Bit Encoding
sections.content:
PHBs and sets of PHBs are encoded in an unsigned 16-bit binary field, arranged in one of two cases.

Case 1 covers PHBs defined by standards action, as per RFC 2474. The encoding for a single PHB is the recommended DSCP value for that PHB, left-justified in the 16-bit field, with bits 6 through 15 set to zero. The recommended DSCP value MUST be used, even if the network in question has chosen a different mapping. The encoding for a set of PHBs is the numerically smallest of the encodings for the various PHBs in the set, with bit 14 set to 1. Thus for the AF1x PHBs, the encoding is that of the AF11 PHB with bit 14 set to 1.

Case 2 covers PHBs not defined by standards action, that is, experimental or local use PHBs as allowed by RFC 2474. An arbitrary 12-bit PHB identification code, assigned by IANA, is placed left-justified in the 16-bit field. Bit 15 is set to 1, and bit 14 is zero for a single PHB or 1 for a set of PHBs. Bits 12 and 13 are zero; they are reserved either for expansion of the PHB identification code, or for other use, at some point in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The 16 bits hold either a standard behaviour or a locally assigned one. Bit 15 says which case it is, and bit 14 says whether the code names one behaviour or a group of them.

sections.title: Sets Must Be Scheduling Classes
sections.content:
In both cases, when a single PHBID is used to identify a set of PHBs, that is, when bit 14 is set to 1, the set of PHBs MUST constitute a PHB Scheduling Class. That means the use of PHBs from the set MUST NOT cause intra-microflow traffic reordering when different PHBs from the set are applied to traffic in the same microflow. The set of AF1x PHBs is an example of a PHB Scheduling Class.

Sets of PHBs that do not constitute a PHB Scheduling Class can be identified by using more than one PHBID.
sections.plainLanguage: One code can only name a group of behaviours that are safe to use together, meaning packets of the same flow must not be reordered by mixing them. A group that does not meet that rule has to be named with several codes instead.

sections.title: Signalling the Class Selector Codepoints
sections.content:
RFC 2474 defines the eight DS codepoint values of the form 'xxx000', where x may be 0 or 1, as the Class Selector Codepoints. Codepoint 000000 is the recommended DSCP value for the Default PHB, and hence the Case 1 PHBID constructed from that codepoint is used to signal the Default PHB.

For convenience and consistent operation with networks that employ IP Precedence, as in RFC 1812, the Case 1 format PHBIDs constructed from the other seven Class Selector Codepoints may also be used to signal PHBs. In each case, the PHB signalled by such a PHBID is the PHB to which the embedded class selector codepoint, or the IP Precedence value that corresponds to it in non-DiffServ domains, is mapped in the recipient's network. Different networks employ different mappings, and RFC 2474 discusses this further.

Any specified use of PHBIDs SHOULD allow the use of the eight Case 1 PHBIDs constructed from the Class Selector Codepoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight of the Diff-Serv codepoints were reserved for class selectors, and the zero value among them stands for the default behaviour. The RFC allows those eight codes to be used to name behaviours too, so that old networks that only understand IP precedence still work.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA is requested to create a new assignment registry for 'Per-Hop Behavior Identification Codes', initially allowing values in the range 0 to 4095 decimal.

Assignment of values in this field requires the identity of the assignee, a brief description of the new PHB with enough detail to distinguish it from existing standardized and non-standardized PHBs, which in the case of a set of PHBs should cover all the PHBs in the set, and a reference to a stable document describing the PHB in detail.

During the first year of existence of this registry, IANA is requested to refer all requests to the IETF DiffServ working group for review. Subsequently, requests should be reviewed by the IETF Transport Area Directors or by an expert they designate. If the number of assignments begins to approach 4096, the Transport Area Directors should be alerted.
sections.plainLanguage: Codes for locally defined behaviours are handed out from a public registry, starting at 4095 and working down. Each request has to describe the new behaviour clearly enough that it cannot be confused with an existing one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the encoding in itself raises no security issues. Users of the encoding should, however, consider that modifying a PHB identification code may constitute theft or denial of service, so protocols that use this encoding must be adequately protected.

Just signalling a PHBID SHOULD NOT be sufficient to grant the sender access to a PHB that it would otherwise not be able to use. Where this is an issue, receivers SHOULD treat received PHBIDs as requests for service, and use local policy to decide whether to grant or deny such requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The code itself is harmless, but changing one in flight could let someone take traffic they should not have. So a receiver should treat a requested behaviour as a request and apply its own policy before granting it.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2836
sections.content: RFC 2836 did not consider the Class Selector code points, which are covered by Section 3 of the present document. A clarification has been added at the end of Section 2 for the case of PHB Scheduling Classes, and the second paragraph of Section 5 has been added.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version left out the class selector codepoints, and this version adds them along with a clearer rule about which groups of behaviours may share one code.
